claims.claim: An idea started by a well-connected scientist reaches half of all 7,678 authors in 9 steps (median of 300 runs); among faculty alone half is reached in 12 steps (64.52% reached by step 15 vs 88.88%).
claims.check: Monte Carlo, same rule and seeds-per-run on both networks; T50 is the censored median over runs

claims.claim: If each person passes an idea on only once with probability 0.2, a large outbreak covers 59% of the full network but only 30% of the faculty-only network: 0.2 is above the full network's measured threshold (0.06) and below the faculty network's (0.215).
claims.check: bond percolation, 100 repeats per T; S = mean largest-cluster share

claims.claim: The textbook threshold <k>/(<k²>−<k>) underestimates the measured one in all 8 networks: the simulated threshold is 1.54–2.32 times the formula, because co-authorship is clustered (clustering 0.7 in the full network) and the formula assumes no clustering.
claims.check: peak of the mean small-outbreak size chi(T) vs the configuration-model formula

claims.claim: The mean-field model (NIMFA) never predicts less spreading than the simulation: across all 28 network × field runs the smallest gap is -0.26 percentage points (simulation noise), the largest 12.49.
claims.check: NIMFA(t) − MC(t) at every step, allowing 0.5 pp of Monte Carlo noise

claims.claim: The simulations are converged: for the top seed in every field, rerunning with 25, 50 and 100 runs changes T50 by at most 0 steps (or leaves it 'not reached' every time) and final reach by at most 0.89 percentage points.
claims.check: T50 within 1 step, reach within 2 pp

claims.claim: Mean field and simulation rank the seeds the same way: Spearman ρ between their early-reach rankings is 0.91–1.00 on the co-authorship networks (median 0.97 over all runs).
When transmission depends on topic overlap, ideas stay in their field: 76.59% of Chemistry researchers adopt by step 15, but only 2.46% of researchers outside Chemistry.
Along paper citations ideas travel only forward in time, so they stay local: from the 15 most-cited papers, 1.68% of the 10,931 papers are reached by step 15 (22 papers sit in citation cycles).
On the faculty network, ideas started by CSIR-IICT faculty spread fastest early on (step-3 reach CSIR-IICT 5.98%, CSIR-NCL 4.92%, CSIR-CECRI 1.23%).
claims.check: simulation and mean field give the same order

claims.claim: Faculty = 382 scientists on the institutes' rosters after removing 123 technical staff, duplicates and page-text entries from 505 scraped entries; 306 have papers in 2016–2026.
The faculty co-authorship network here is the main dashboard's: 238 scientists, 627 co-author pairs.

In the labs' real citations an idea passes over a co-authorship tie with probability 0.81% on average, and 4.95% for the most reused ideas (cited by 10 or more lab papers): below the tipping point measured for the full network (6%) and far below the faculty network's (21.5%). 79% of the 511,832 works the labs cite are cited by one lab paper only.
claims.check: per-tie transmissibility of all ideas and of the most reused ones both below the full network's measured tipping point

claims.claim: Measured on real citations, a tie of a student or other non-faculty author passes an idea on 2.7× as often as a faculty member's tie (1.51% vs 0.56%; 2.3–2.6× within every reuse group), but a faculty member has 35 co-authors on average against 5.6.
claims.check: ratio above 1 in every reuse group and faculty have more co-authors

claims.claim: Ideas travel with people: in 78% of real pass-ons an earlier user is an author of the new paper. One co-author who used an idea makes a researcher only slightly more likely to use it on their own (0.038% a year vs 0.032% for researchers in the same subfield without such a co-author, 1.17×); three or more raise it 3.5×.
claims.check: carried share above 50% and the independent-adoption lift grows from one to three or more adopting co-authors

claims.claim: The three labs are islands that learn from abroad by reading: 1.44% of co-authorship ties link people of different labs, and when a paper of the foreign twins is cited by a second lab, a person links it to the first lab's users in only 3.8% of cases (the labs' own papers: 22.8%). The labs cite 4,461 papers of their 9 foreign peers but co-authored 49 with them.
claims.check: cross-lab ties under 5%, foreign ideas reach other labs through a person in under 10% of cases and less often than the labs' own papers
